claim: DFV-B is a dual fluorescent reporter virus derived from HIV-1 NL4-3 strain with GFP expression controlled by LTR and mCherry expression controlled by EF-1α promoter.
source: To specifically identify latently infected cells, we constructed a new reporter virus by engineering GFP and mCherry into the HIV-1 genome, in which GFP expression was controlled by LTR, while mCherry expression was independently controlled by the constitutive promoter EF-1α. This viral construct was named DFV-B (dual fluorescent virus-B) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the construction of DFV-B and Figure 1A shows the genomic structure diagram.

claim: DFV-B infection of activated primary CD4+ T cells produces productively infected (double-positive) cells at roughly 16 times the frequency of latently infected (single mCherry-positive) cells on day 3 post-infection.
source: Productively infected (double-positive, DP) and latently infected (single mCherry-positive, mC) CD4+ T cells were clearly distinguishable (Figure 1B), and the percentage of the DP cells was roughly 16 times more than the single mC-positive cells on day 3 post-infection (p.i.) in STCM (Super T cell medium) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from DFV-B infection experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When DFV-B-infected cells are transferred to cytokine-free medium, the proportion of double-positive cells decreases while the proportion of single mCherry-positive cells increases over time.
source: As culture time increased, the proportion of DP cells decreased significantly, while the proportion of mC cells gradually increased (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations shown in Figure 1C tracking cell populations over time.

claim: Single mCherry-positive cells account for up to 30% of total infected cells on day 10 post-infection in cytokine-free medium.
source: mC cells accounted for up to 30% of the total infected cells on day 10 p.i. (Figure 1C), suggesting some of the productively infected cells survived, reverted to a more resting state, and turned off viral gene (GFP) expression, which may add to the increased proportion of latently infected cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from Figure 1C at day 10 post-infection.

claim: More than 50% of sorted single mCherry-positive cells can be reactivated by PMA and ionomycin stimulation.
source: Compared to the DMSO control, over 50% of total cells were converted from mC to DP cells (Figure 2B), suggesting that more than half of the latently infected cells were reactivated.
evidence: The manuscript reports reactivation data from sorted mC cells shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Double-positive cells transcribe significantly higher amounts of HIV-1 mRNA than single mCherry-positive cells, nearly 10 times as much.
source: As expected, the DP cells transcribed significantly higher amounts of HIV-1 mRNA, nearly 10 times as the mC cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data comparing HIV-1 mRNA levels shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HIV-1 Gag and Vif proteins are detected in double-positive cells but not in single mCherry-positive cells.
source: HIV-1 Gag and Vif protein production were detected by western blot in DP cells, but not in mC cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports western blot results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP-DNA and mCherry-DNA levels are comparable between single mCherry-positive and double-positive cells, indicating no difference in viral integration.
source: Comparing to the uninfected DN cells, both GFP-DNA and mCherry-DNA were comparable between mC and DP cells, indicating no difference in viral integration (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data for integrated DNA shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GFP mRNA levels in double-positive cells are much higher than in single mCherry-positive cells, while mCherry mRNA levels remain the same.
source: Meanwhile, levels of GFP mRNA in DP cells were much higher than that in mC cells, but mCherry mRNA levels remained the same (Figure 2E), consistent with the phenotypes observed by FACS.
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data for mRNA levels shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Single mCherry-positive cells express significantly lower levels of activation markers (CD25, CD69, HLA-DR) than double-positive cells.
source: mC cells expressed significantly lower levels of activation markers and exhaustion markers than DP cells (Figure 3C and D), again supporting our results that mC cells were latently infected.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data for activation markers shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Single mCherry-positive cells express significantly lower levels of exhaustion markers (PD-1, TIM-3) than double-positive cells.
source: mC cells expressed significantly lower levels of activation markers and exhaustion markers than DP cells (Figure 3C and D), again supporting our results that mC cells were latently infected.
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data for exhaustion markers shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The ratio of single mCherry-positive cells to total infected cells increases from 15.7% to 64.8% when infection occurs during effector-to-memory transition.
source: In general, EMT CD4+ T cells were less permissive to DFV-B infection; however, the ratio of mC cells to total infected cells (mC+DP) steadily increased from 15.7% (day 0 infection) to 64.8% (day 10 infection) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from infections at different time points shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Over 80% of single mCherry-positive Jurkat cells are converted to double-positive cells following TNF-α treatment.
source: Over 80% of mC cells were converted to DP cells following the treatment, but DP and DN cells were not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), confirming DFV-B infection could directly identify latent infection in Jurkat cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports reactivation data from Jurkat cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: J-mC cells can be efficiently activated by JQ1, SAHA, TNF-α, PMA, and PMA plus ionomycin to express both fluorescent proteins.
source: As expected, J-mC cells were activated efficiently by all stimuli to express both fluorescent proteins (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports reactivation data for J-mC cells with various stimuli shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: PMA treatment induces significant increases in HIV-1 gag, tat, vif, and LTR mRNA expression in J-mC cells.
source: The potent induction of cell-associated HIV-1 mRNA after PMA treatment further confirmed the integrated proviruses were reactivated in this model (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data for HIV-1 mRNA after PMA treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: J-mC cells maintain relatively stable mRNA expression levels and DNA levels of GFP and mCherry over the course of a year.
source: Besides, mRNA expression levels and DNA levels of GFP and mCherry remained relatively stable over the course of a year (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The manuscript reports long-term tracking data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: 49.09% of integration sites in mixed J-Lat 8.4 and 15.4 cells are located at position 77946384 of chromosome 1.
source: As shown in Figure 5A and B, 49.09% of the integration sites were located in the same position 77946384 of chromosome 1% and 46.92% counts were located in the same position 34441293 of chromosome 19 (Supplementary file 1), which were exactly the integration sites of J-Lat 8.4 and J-Lat 15.4, suggesting that LAM-HTGTS was a robust method for analyzing HIV-1 integration sites.
evidence: The manuscript reports LAM-HTGTS validation data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: 46.92% of integration sites in mixed J-Lat 8.4 and 15.4 cells are located at position 34441293 of chromosome 19.
source: As shown in Figure 5A and B, 49.09% of the integration sites were located in the same position 77946384 of chromosome 1% and 46.92% counts were located in the same position 34441293 of chromosome 19 (Supplementary file 1), which were exactly the integration sites of J-Lat 8.4 and J-Lat 15.4, suggesting that LAM-HTGTS was a robust method for analyzing HIV-1 integration sites.
evidence: The manuscript reports LAM-HTGTS validation data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: J-mC cells have integration sites diffusely distributed on 24 chromosomes.
source: For J-mC cells, all integration sites recovered were diffusely distributed on 24 chromosomes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports LAM-HTGTS data for J-mC cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Chromosome 17 harbors the most abundant and diverse integration sites in J-mC cells.
source: Chromosome 17 harbored the most abundant integration sites, which at the same time were extremely diverse (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports LAM-HTGTS data for chromosome 17 shown in Figure 5D.

claim: More than 70% of integration sites in J-mC cells are distributed in intronic regions.
source: We also noticed that more than 70% of the integration sites were distributed on intronic regions (Figure 5E), which is consistent with previous reports on integration sites recovered from ART-treated HIV-1 infected individuals (Han et al., 2004; Cohn et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports LAM-HTGTS data shown in Figure 5E and cites previous studies.

claim: HIV-1 proviruses in J-mC cells are enriched in genes related to 'Regulation of transcription', 'Membrane', and 'Binding'.
source: We performed gene ontology (GO) and GO pathway analysis on the genes at all integration sites, and found that the proviruses were enriched in genes related to 'Regulation of transcription', 'Membrane', and 'Binding' (Figure 5F).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO analysis results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: HIV-1 integrates more frequently in cancer-related pathways in J-mC cells.
source: In addition, HIV-1 integrated more frequently in cancer-related pathways (Figure 5G), which is also consistent with previously reported ex vivo data (Wagner et al., 2014; Cohn et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 5G and cites previous studies.

claim: High-throughput screening with J-mC cells identified previously reported latency reversing agents including SAHA, panobinostat, and romidepsin.
source: The screening was performed from high concentrations to low concentrations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and with this system we successfully identified several previously reported LRAs, including SAHA, panobinostat, and romidepsin (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports drug screening results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ACY-1215 (ricolinistat) was discovered as a novel compound that reactivates latent HIV-1 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: A new compound, ricolinistat (ACY-1215), was discovered in this screen (Figure 6A and B), displaying excellent potential to reactivate latent HIV-1 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports drug screening and dose-response data shown in Figures 6A, 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ACY-1215 induces an eight-fold increase in viral transcription in J-mC cells after 24 hours of treatment.
source: Viral transcription was induced eight fold in average after 24 hr of ACY-1215 treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data for HIV-1 mRNA after ACY-1215 treatment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ACY-1215 shows better latency reversing activities in J-mC cells than in different J-Lat cell lines.
source: In addition, we found that ACY-1215 showed better latency reversing activities in J-mC cells than in different J-Lat cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E), which probably explained why it was not discovered in previous drug screenings.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative reactivation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: ACY-1215 displays a synergistic effect with several other latency reversing agents, but not disulfiram.
source: Besides, we observed that ACY-1215 displayed a synergistic effect with several other LRAs, but not disulfiram (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports combination treatment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ACY-1215 is less toxic than SAHA as measured by annexin-V/propidium iodide staining and CCK-8 assay.
source: ACY-1215 is an oral HDAC6-selective inhibitor, and our data suggested that it was less toxic than SAHA as measured by annexin-V/propidium iodide (PI) staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) and CCK-8 assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: ACY-1215 does not induce upregulation of classic T cell activation markers on freshly isolated primary CD4+ T cells.
source: ACY-1215 does not induce upregulation of classic T cell activation markers on freshly isolated primary CD4+ T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data for activation markers shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ACY-1215 has no significant effect on CCR5 and CXCR4 expression of CD4+ T cells.
source: In addition, ACY-1215 had no significant effect on CCR5 and CXCR4 expression of CD4+ T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data for co-receptor expression shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and 3C.

claim: No significant induction of IFN-γ and TNF-α is detected in CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells following ACY-1215 treatment.
source: No significant induction of IFN-γ and TNF-α was detected in CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells from the same donors following ACY-1215 treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D–G.

claim: ACY-1215 reactivates over 80% of latent HIV-1 in Bcl-2-transduced CD4+ T cells when compared to PMA and ionomycin.
source: At 48 hr post-treatment, we found that ACY-1215 worked as well as SAHA, reactivating over 80% of latent HIV-1 when comparing to PMA and ionomycin (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports reactivation data from Bcl-2-transduced cells shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: ACY-1215 induces an average 50-fold increase in cell-associated HIV-1 mRNA in CD4+ T cells from ART-suppressed infected individuals.
source: As shown in the Figure 6G and H, ACY-1215 robustly induced the level of cell-associated HIV-1 mRNA by an average of 50-fold comparing to the negative controls.
evidence: The manuscript reports viral quality assurance data from patient samples shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: DFV-B displays a lower percentage of single GFP positive cells (<1%) than previously reported dual reporter viral systems.
source: Compared with the previously reported infection models, DFV-B displayed a better infection profile with a clearer cell population and a lower percentage of single GFP positive cells (<1%) (Figure 1B) than RGH (Dahabieh et al., 2013), Duo-Fluo I (Calvanese et al., 2013), mdHIV (Hashemi et al., 2016), and HIVGKO (Battivelli et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript compares DFV-B to previously reported systems with citations.

claim: More than 50% of latently infected primary cells by DFV-B are reactivatable by PMA and ionomycin, compared to only 5% in the HIVGKO model.
source: More than 50% of the latently infected primary cells by DFV-B were reactivated by PMA and ionomycin in CFM (Figure 2B), while only 5% were reactivatable in the HIVGKO model (Battivelli et al., 2018), indicating the robustness of the DFV-B system to research the mechanism of HIV-1 latency maintenance and reactivation in vitro.
evidence: The manuscript compares reactivation rates between DFV-B and HIVGKO with citation.

claim: The latent HIV-1 reservoir mainly resides in resting memory CD4+ T cells.
source: The latent HIV-1 reservoir mainly resides in resting memory CD4+ T cells (Chun et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1997; Chomont et al., 2009), but they are normally not the direct targets for infection, due to the blocks in reverse transcription (Korin and Zack, 1998), integration (Bukrinsky et al., 1992) and host restriction by SAMHD1 (Baldauf et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established knowledge.

claim: HIV-1 latency is preferentially established in effector-to-memory transitioning CD4+ T cells.
source: It has been recently demonstrated that HIV-1 latency was preferentially established in EMT CD4+ T cells (Shan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study demonstrating this finding.

claim: ACY-1215 is an oral HDAC6-selective inhibitor.
source: ACY-1215 is an oral HDAC6-selective inhibitor, and our data suggested that it was less toxic than SAHA as measured by annexin-V/propidium iodide (PI) staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) and CCK-8 assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript describes ACY-1215 as an HDAC6-selective inhibitor, which is established knowledge about this compound.

claim: ACY-1215 has completed Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials for treatment of multiple myeloma.
source: ACY-1215, an orally bioavailable HDAC6-selective inhibitor, had previously completed Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials for treatment of multiple myeloma (Santo et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting clinical trial completion.

claim: ACY-1215 selectively increases acetylated α-tubulin without altering acetylated histone H4 at biologically relevant concentrations (<10 μM).
source: In vitro, ACY-1215 selectively increased acetylated a-tubulin (a marker of HDAC6 inhibition) without altering acetylated histone H4 (a marker of global HDAC inhibition) at biologically relevant concentrations (<10 μM) (Carew et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting ACY-1215's selective effects.

claim: HDAC6-KO mice are normal, as opposed to the lethal effect of genetic ablation of class I HDACs.
source: Besides, HDAC6-KO mice were normal, as opposed to the lethal effect of genetic ablation of class I HDACs (Haberland et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting the viability of HDAC6-KO mice.

claim: ACY-1215 and ACY-241 can downregulate Th2 cytokine production, decrease T-cell exhaustion, increase T-cell killing ability, and augment the proportion of central memory cells.
source: ACY-1215 and ACY-241 (another HDAC6-selective inhibitor) can downregulate Th2 cytokine production, decrease T-cell exhaustion, increase T-cell killing ability, and augment the proportion of central memory cells and expression of cytolytic markers in vitro (Laino et al., 2019; Bae et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies reporting these effects of ACY-1215 and ACY-241.

claim: ACY-1215 can change the chromatin accessibility of T cells.
source: ACY-1215 can also change the chromatin accessibility of T cells (Laino et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting this effect of ACY-1215.

claim: ACY-1215 has anti-inflammatory effect and is considered a potential anti-inflammatory drug.
source: Besides, ACY-1215 has anti-inﬂammatory eﬀect and is considered a potential anti-inflammatory drug (Cheng et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies reporting ACY-1215's anti-inflammatory properties.

claim: ACY-1215 can prevent the neurotoxicity of HIV-1 envelope protein gp120.
source: A recent study reported that ACY-1215 could prevent the neurotoxicity of HIV-1 envelope protein gp120 (Wenzel et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study reporting this neuroprotective effect.

claim: Latently infected CD4+ T cells harbor transcriptionally silent but replication-competent proviral genomes.
source: These latently infected cells harbor transcriptional silent but replication-competent proviral genome, which was demonstrated to be the origin of rapid viral rebound after ART is interrupted (Finzi et al., 1997; Chun et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies establishing this characteristic of latently infected cells.

claim: Latently infected cells are the origin of rapid viral rebound after ART is interrupted.
source: These latently infected cells harbor transcriptional silent but replication-competent proviral genome, which was demonstrated to be the origin of rapid viral rebound after ART is interrupted (Finzi et al., 1997; Chun et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating this role of latently infected cells.

claim: Latently infected CD4+ T cells are essentially indistinguishable from uninfected cells and are not recognized by immune responses.
source: Latently infected CD4+ T cells are essentially indistinguishable from uninfected cells and are therefore not recognized by immune responses, including broadly neutralizing antibodies or cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about latently infected cells.

claim: Current technologies do not allow direct identification or purification of live latently infected cells from infected individuals on ART.
source: Current technologies also do not allow direct identification or purification of live latently infected cells from the infected individuals on ART.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a current limitation in the field.

claim: The difficulty in distinguishing latently infected cells from uninfected cells has represented a major bottleneck precluding comprehensive understandings of HIV-1 latency.
source: The difficulty in distinguishing latently infected cells from the vast majority of uninfected cells has represented a major bottleneck precluding comprehensive understandings of HIV-1 latency.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a recognized challenge in the field.

claim: Previously reported dual reporter virus systems have apparent defects when infecting primary CD4+ T cells, including unclear cell subpopulations.
source: However, some apparent defects existed with the previously reported systems, especially when infecting primary CD4+ T cells: (a) unclear cell subpopulations, for example, the boundaries of productively infected cells were obscured (Calvanese et al., 2013; Battivelli et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and identifies their limitations.

claim: Previously reported dual reporter virus systems have potential interference of cytokines on HIV-1 latency.
source: (b) potential interference of cytokines on HIV-1 latency, as all infected cells (Dahabieh et al., 2013; Battivelli et al., 2018) were maintained in IL-2 containing medium for latency establishment
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and identifies their limitations.

claim: Only 5% of HIVGKO cells were reactivated by bryostatin-1 and panobinostat.
source: (c) low frequency of reactivation of the identified latently infected cells, for instance, only 5% of HIVGKO cells were reactivated by bryostatin-1 and panobinostat (Battivelli et al., 2018), which bona fide limit its application to explore the mechanism of HIV latency maintenance and reactivation in vitro.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study reporting low reactivation rates.

claim: J-Lat cell line models are derived from single-cell clones with identical integration sites.
source: Although some cell line models of HIV-1 latency (such as the widely used J-Lat model) have been reported, all of which are derived from single-cell clones, and therefore with identical integration sites, which significantly underrepresented the heterogenous nature of latently infected cells in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript describes a known limitation of J-Lat models.

claim: J-mC cells harbor tremendously diverse HIV-1 integration sites that are highly physiologically relevant.
source: Together, these data clearly demonstrated that J-mC cells harbored tremendously diverse HIV-1 integration sites, which were highly physiologically relevant, suggesting this cell line model as a valuable tool to study HIV-1 latency.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the integration site analysis data and draws this conclusion.

claim: DFV-B infection circumvents the clonal-derived biases of previous cell lines like J-Lat.
source: We also showed that DFV-B infection in Jurkat cells can generate a bunch of stable latently infected cells (named J-mC cells), which were obtained by natural infection, therefore circumventing the clonal-derived biases of some previous cell lines like J-Lat.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an advantage of the DFV-B system based on the method of generation.

claim: ACY-1215 has a higher safety and tolerability profile than pan-HDAC inhibitors such as SAHA or panobinostat.
source: As an oral HDAC6-selective inhibitor, ACY-1215 has a higher safety and tolerability profile than the currently available pan-HDAC inhibitors such as SAHA or panobinastat, making it a promising LRA in future applications for HIV-1 functional cure.
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about ACY-1215's safety profile and draws this conclusion.

claim: Selective HDAC6 inhibition stops aggresome formation and inhibits degradation leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins.
source: Selective HDAC6 inhibition stops aggresome formation, thence inhibiting the degradation leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins within cells, and may reduce the toxicity related to the off-target effects of pan-HDAC inhibitors (Amengual et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study explaining the mechanism of HDAC6 inhibition.

claim: The proportion of single GFP-positive cells decreased from 0.7% to 0.2% as culture time increased.
source: A small fraction of single GFP+ cells existed after DFV-B infection (Figure 1B), and we traced and found that the proportion of single GFP+ cells decreased from 0.7% to 0.2% (similar to uninfected cells) as the culture time increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which is significantly lower than the previous reported dual reporter viral systems (Calvanese et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports tracking data for single GFP+ cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The integrated DNA levels of GFP and mCherry in single GFP+ cells are not different.
source: The integrated DNA levels of GFP and mCherry in this single GFP+ cells were not different (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting both reporters were still stably integrated.
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data for integrated DNA shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The absence of GFP production in single mCherry-positive cells is due to viral latency but not genomic deletion.
source: To further verify that the absence of GFP production was due to viral latency but not possible genomic deletion, we quantified the cell-associated DNA and RNA of fluorescent protein from different populations respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes experiments designed to test this hypothesis and presents supporting data in Figure 2E.

claim: The viability of single mCherry-positive cell population was more than 40% during the reactivation process.
source: During this process, the viability of mC cell population was more than 40% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Primary CD4+ T cells are in the process of effector-to-memory transition after 5-7 days in cytokine-free medium culture.
source: We first confirmed the primary CD4+ T cells were in the process of EMT after 5–7 days in CFM culture, as the expression of CD25/CD69/HLA-DR and T cell exhaustion markers (PD-1 and TIM-3) had been greatly reduced (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports flow cytometry data confirming EMT shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Effector-to-memory transitioning CD4+ T cells are less permissive to DFV-B infection.
source: In general, EMT CD4+ T cells were less permissive to DFV-B infection; however, the ratio of mC cells to total infected cells (mC+DP) steadily increased from 15.7% (day 0 infection) to 64.8% (day 10 infection) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript reports infection data at different time points shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A total of 5154 identified integration sites were obtained from J-mC cells.
source: C: Chromosome distribution of all integration sites. A total of 5154 identified integration sites were obtained from J-mC cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of integration sites identified in Figure 5C legend.

claim: A total of 499 identified integration sites were obtained from chromosome 17 in J-mC cells.
source: D: Distribution of integration sites on chromosome 17. The percentage of top 10 integration sites was shown. A total of 499 identified integration sites were obtained from chromosome 17.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of integration sites on chromosome 17 in Figure 5D legend.

claim: DFV-B has a portion of env deleted for a single round of infection.
source: Of note, a portion of env was deleted for a single round of infection of the virus, and the vpr gene had a frameshift mutation to reduce the toxicity of the pseudovirus.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modifications made to construct DFV-B.

claim: DFV-B has a frameshift mutation in the vpr gene to reduce toxicity.
source: Of note, a portion of env was deleted for a single round of infection of the virus, and the vpr gene had a frameshift mutation to reduce the toxicity of the pseudovirus.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modifications made to construct DFV-B.

claim: Most of the nef sequence in DFV-B was replaced by GFP-EF-1α-kozak-mCherry, with 31 bp of nef sequence reserved.
source: Most of the nef sequence was replaced by GFP- EF-1α-kozak-mCherry, and the remaining 31 bp of nef sequence was reserved in order not to disturb the function of LTR.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modifications made to construct DFV-B.

claim: The 31 bp of nef sequence was reserved in DFV-B in order not to disturb the function of LTR.
source: Most of the nef sequence was replaced by GFP- EF-1α-kozak-mCherry, and the remaining 31 bp of nef sequence was reserved in order not to disturb the function of LTR.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for retaining part of the nef sequence.
